title: Ang 1118–1124: Kedara
tomorrow: after an evening raga, what does the morning sing first?

segments.voice: Yesterday, winter songs: the night as a watch, not a waste, in Nanak's chhant and in Psalm 130. Today the light goes gold, and the whole week comes home.

The porch at the end of a long day. Shoes off, the street going quiet, the sky turning the color of chai. That's the hour this week lands in. A grandmother's couplet at the door: when You are on my side. A warrior who never leaves the field. A canopy over the one the world shunned. A raga of courage, walked end to end. A year of months, each one a letter. A long night kept as a watch. Six days. And now Kedara, a short raga that tradition gives to the evening.
screen: `THE PORCH, THE GOLD HOUR.` → `SIX DAYS COME HOME.` → `KEDARA, FOR EVENING.`

segments.voice: Kedara opens on ang 1118 with Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, and his first line is, in paraphrase: O my mind, sing the Name of the Lord, every day. Not once, after a big moment. Every day, including the ordinary ones. Then, near the end, two Bhagats. Kabir, on ang 1123, in paraphrase: let go of both praise and slander, give up pride. Ravidas, on ang 1124: a family full of rituals means little if devotion isn't in the heart. Put the three together and you get an evening checklist. Let the day's compliments and insults both go. Don't lean on where you come from. Sing the Name, and come back tomorrow. That's what's left to sing when the day is done. Not a scoreboard of who praised you and who didn't, but a refrain you can pick up again in the morning. Evening.
screen: `RAM DAS: SING IT EVERY DAY.` · `KABIR: DROP PRAISE AND BLAME.` · `RAVIDAS: DEVOTION IN THE HEART.` · `NOT A SCOREBOARD, A REFRAIN.` · then, large: `EVENING.`

segments.voice: Look toward the nearest window or the softest light in the room, and just watch it for the whole sit. Let one compliment from this week go, and one sting too, as the light settles.
Ang 1118. Where raga Kedara opens with Guru Ram Das: O my mind, sing the Name every day.
Your line: evening, when praise and blame both go and the refrain stays. That's two weeks, and fifteen-eighty-two.
